objects_methods.notes: types_and_methods is the bridge from built-in methods to self (obj.method(x) == Class.method(obj, x)). isinstance (B02/B05 handoff) is isinstance_checks; isinstance with subclasses is B12 inheritance, which should encompass it. B08 recursion.nested_lists used type(x) == list and can now switch to isinstance in a stitch. object_references owns aliasing of user-defined objects (B06 handoff); objects as attributes of other objects ('has-a', Helsinki Part 9) is B12 composition. Canvas object methods (Code in Place) belong to the graphics batch.

classes.notes: Seven topics: define_and_instantiate, then (after instance_attributes.set_and_read and constructors.init_sets_attributes) the method topics, collections of objects, records_as_classes (data abstraction, B05 handoff, plus to_dict for B10's serialisation handoff) and dataclasses (B07 handoff). CapWords naming (B01 handoff) is define_and_instantiate KP3. dataclasses is non-core with no taught_in (none of the 8 courses teaches it) but is the modern record type; B12 sum_types may want it as a prerequisite, which would justify promoting it to core. Class patterns in match (B04 handoff, case Point(x=0)) were NOT written here: they fit B12 sum_types, which runs in parallel; if B12 did not write them, a stitch should add a KP to classes.dataclasses or enums.enums_in_logic. Project-shaped class work (Quiz Game, Coffee Machine, Asteroids) is multistep material. unittest_module (B09, pending concept:classes) can now depend on classes.define_methods.

instance_attributes.notes: set_and_read comes before __init__ (Helsinki/py4e order) and motivates it with the silent-typo bug. getattr/setattr/hasattr/vars (codecademy 'Attribute Functions') are a non-core topic. __slots__ was left out.

constructors.notes: init_sets_attributes, defaults_and_derived (includes the mutable default in __init__, encompassing B05 parameters_arguments.mutable_default_trap as non_ancestor because that topic is non-core) and validate_in_init (B09 handoff: raising in constructors). __del__/object lifecycle (py4e) was left out. Custom exception classes with their own __init__ and super().__init__ need inheritance and belong to B12, which should encompass raising_exceptions.custom_exceptions (B09 asked for this). Reconciliation: defaults_and_derived now depends on parameters_arguments.mutable_default_trap (promoted to core) instead of a non_ancestor encompassing.

class_attributes.notes: Owns @classmethod and @staticmethod (B08 handoff). classmethods also owns from_dict, the partner of classes.records_as_classes' to_dict (B10 serialisation handoff). @classmethod is taught as a marker line; decorators.at_syntax is not a prerequisite here (it is for encapsulation.read_only_properties). Why cls instead of the class name (subclasses) is for B12 inheritance. staticmethods is non-core (cs50p only).

encapsulation.notes: private_by_convention (_x, __x name mangling, getter/setter methods), read_only_properties and property_setters (@property, B08 handoff, built on decorators.at_syntax). The OOP 'abstraction' pillar as interface vs implementation is classes.records_as_classes KP3; abstract base classes are B12 abstract_classes.

dunder_methods.notes: Six topics: str_and_repr, equality_and_ordering and operator_overloading are core; container_methods, custom_iterators (B04 iteration handoff) and context_manager_protocol (B10 handoff: __enter__/__exit__) are non-core. __hash__ (an object with __eq__ becomes unhashable) was not given a KP because sets/dicts are not ancestors of equality_and_ordering; classes.dataclasses KP4 mentions that frozen dataclasses are hashable. functools.total_ordering, __call__, __bool__ (only the __len__ fallback is taught), __iadd__ and __radd__/sum() were left out. Overriding dunder methods as polymorphism is B12.

enums.notes: Two non-core topics (bootdev only). define_and_use and enums_in_logic (match on members, the B04 match handoff for value patterns; auto() and StrEnum). Named constants for magic numbers stay with B02 constants; enums_in_logic encompasses nothing from it. Sum types built from enums or dataclasses are B12 sum_types, which should list enums.define_and_use as a prerequisite. Flag and IntEnum were left out. 'from enum import Enum' is a memorised line before B13 modules_imports.

topics.title: Every value is an object: types and methods
topics.summary: Use type() to see the class of any value, explain that methods come from that class, and read obj.method(x) as Class.method(obj, x).

knowledge_points.title: type() names the class of a value
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(type("hi"))
print(type([1, 2]))
print(type(3.5))
Every value is an object, and its type is a class: str, list, float.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what type() prints for literals and variables of six built-in types.

knowledge_points.title: Methods belong to the type
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("hi".upper())   # HI
n = 5
n.upper()
A method is a function stored on the class; int has no upper, so Python raises AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'upper'.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict whether each call works or raises AttributeError; use dir() to check whether a type has a method.

knowledge_points.title: obj.method(x) means Class.method(obj, x)
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(str.upper("hi"))   # HI
nums = [3]
list.append(nums, 4)
print(nums)              # [3, 4]
The object before the dot is passed in as the method's first argument. This is where self will come from.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite dotted calls in Class.method(obj, ...) form and back; predict the result.

knowledge_points.title: Calling a class makes a new object
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(type(int))      # <class 'type'>
print(int("7") + 1)   # 8
letters = list("ab")
print(letters)        # ['a', 'b']
int, str and list are classes; calling one builds a new object of that class.
knowledge_points.practice: Classify names as classes or functions; predict the object a class call produces.

topics.title: Checking a value's type with isinstance()
topics.summary: Use isinstance() with one class or a tuple of classes to branch on a value's type, and know why it beats type(x) == ... (including the bool-is-an-int surprise).

knowledge_points.title: isinstance(value, Class)
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(isinstance(5, int))     # True
print(isinstance("5", int))   # False
isinstance answers 'is this value an object of that class?' with True or False.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict True/False for a table of values and classes.

knowledge_points.title: Several allowed types: a tuple of classes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 2.5
print(isinstance(x, (int, float)))   # True
print(isinstance("2.5", (int, float)))  # False
A tuple of classes means 'any of these'.
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the class tuple that accepts the described values; predict results.

knowledge_points.title: isinstance vs type(x) ==, and bool is an int
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(isinstance(True, int))   # True
print(type(True) == int)       # False
print(True + True)             # 2
bool is a kind of int, so isinstance says yes while an exact type check says no; to reject booleans, check bool first.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict both checks for several values; fix a number check that wrongly accepts True.

knowledge_points.title: Branching on the type in a function
knowledge_points.practice: Write a function that handles numbers and strings differently; reorder a wrong elif chain.

topics.title: Defining a class and creating objects from it
topics.summary: Write a class statement, create instances by calling the class, and tell a class from an instance.

knowledge_points.title: A class statement and one instance
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Dog:
    pass

rex = Dog()
print(type(rex))
class Dog: makes a new type; calling Dog() creates an object (an instance) of it.
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in a class statement and the line that creates an instance; predict what type() prints.

knowledge_points.title: Every call makes a new, separate object
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Dog:
    pass

a = Dog()
b = Dog()
print(a == b)   # False
print(a)        # <__main__.Dog object at 0x...> (address varies)
Two calls give two distinct objects; the default printout shows the class and a memory address.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict how many objects a snippet creates and whether two names refer to equal objects.

knowledge_points.title: Vocabulary and naming: class, instance, CapWords
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class BankAccount:      # class names use CapWords
    pass

my_account = BankAccount()   # instance names use snake_case
The class is the blueprint (BankAccount); each object made from it is an instance.
knowledge_points.practice: Label names in a snippet as class or instance; pick the PEP 8 name for a described class.

knowledge_points.title: Forgetting the parentheses
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Dog:
    pass

rex = Dog
print(rex)   # <class '__main__.Dog'>
Without (), rex names the class itself, not a new dog.
knowledge_points.practice: Spot the line that refers to the class instead of creating an instance.

topics.title: Attributes: data stored on an object
topics.summary: Store values on an object with dot assignment, read and update them, and recognise AttributeError and the silent typo bug.

knowledge_points.title: Assign and read with a dot
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Dog:
    pass

rex = Dog()
rex.name = "Rex"
rex.age = 3
print(rex.name, rex.age)   # Rex 3
obj.attr = value stores a value on that one object; obj.attr reads it back.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict printed attributes; write the lines that store two given attributes.

knowledge_points.title: Each object has its own attributes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Dog:
    pass

rex = Dog()
mia = Dog()
rex.age = 3
mia.age = 5
rex.age += 1
print(rex.age, mia.age)   # 4 5
Changing rex's attribute leaves mia's untouched.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace attribute values of two objects through a sequence of updates.

knowledge_points.title: Reading a missing attribute raises AttributeError
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Dog:
    pass

rex = Dog()
rex.name = "Rex"
print(rex.nme)
Python raises AttributeError: 'Dog' object has no attribute 'nme'. Did you mean: 'name'?
knowledge_points.practice: Predict whether each read prints a value or raises AttributeError.

knowledge_points.title: A typo when assigning silently creates a new attribute
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Dog:
    pass

rex = Dog()
rex.age = 3
rex.agee = 4
print(rex.age)   # 3
Assignment never fails, so a misspelt name adds a second attribute; __init__ (next) gives every object the same attributes from the start.
knowledge_points.practice: Find the typo that makes an update have no effect.

topics.title: Setting up new objects with __init__
topics.summary: Write an __init__ method that takes parameters and stores them on self, create objects with arguments, and fix the classic constructor mistakes.

knowledge_points.title: __init__ runs automatically when an object is created
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Dog:
    def __init__(self):
        print("a dog is born")
        self.tricks = 0

rex = Dog()        # a dog is born
print(rex.tricks)  # 0
self is the new object; Python calls __init__ for you right after creating it.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what creating two objects prints; fill in the self.attribute line.

knowledge_points.title: Constructor parameters become attributes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

rex = Dog("Rex", 3)
print(rex.name, rex.age)   # Rex 3
The arguments in Dog(...) go to the parameters after self; self is filled in for you.
knowledge_points.practice: Write a class whose constructor stores three given values; match arguments to parameters.

knowledge_points.title: Passing the wrong number of arguments
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which creation calls succeed; read the TypeError to say which argument is missing.

knowledge_points.title: Bugs: forgetting self. and misspelling __init__
knowledge_points.practice: Fix constructors with a missing self., a misspelt __init__, or a missing self parameter.

topics.title: Default values and starting state in __init__
topics.summary: Give constructor parameters defaults, start attributes that are not parameters, compute attributes from others, and avoid the shared mutable default.

knowledge_points.title: Default parameter values
knowledge_points.practice: Predict attribute values for calls with and without the optional argument.

knowledge_points.title: Attributes that always start the same
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Account:
    def __init__(self, owner):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = 0
        self.history = []

acct = Account("Ann")
print(acct.balance, acct.history)   # 0 []
Not every attribute needs a parameter: starting state can be set directly.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which attributes should be parameters and which start fixed; write the constructor.

knowledge_points.title: Computed attributes do not update themselves
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Rect:
    def __init__(self, w, h):
        self.w = w
        self.h = h
        self.area = w * h

r = Rect(2, 3)
r.w = 10
print(r.area)   # 6
area was calculated once, in __init__; it goes stale when w changes. A method (or later a property) fixes this.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict derived attributes after later changes; choose between storing and computing.

knowledge_points.title: The shared mutable default
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Team:
    def __init__(self, members=[]):
        self.members = members

a = Team()
b = Team()
a.members.append("Ann")
print(b.members)   # ['Ann']
The one default list is shared by every Team; use members=None and create a new list inside __init__.
knowledge_points.practice: Spot the shared default and rewrite it with None.

topics.title: Objects are shared, not copied
topics.summary: Predict the effects of aliasing your own objects: two names for one object, objects passed to functions, and the same object repeated in a list.

knowledge_points.title: Two names, one object
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Counter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.count = 0

a = Counter()
b = a
b.count += 5
print(a.count, a is b)   # 5 True
Assignment copies the reference, not the object, exactly as with lists.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict attribute values after changes made through an alias.

knowledge_points.title: Functions receive the object itself
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which function calls affect the caller's object.

knowledge_points.title: The same object repeated in a list
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Counter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.count = 0

counters = [Counter()] * 3
counters[0].count = 9
print(counters[2].count)   # 9
[obj] * 3 repeats one object three times; build separate objects with a loop instead.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a list that should hold separate objects; predict the shared result.

topics.title: From dictionaries to classes: data abstraction
topics.summary: Turn a dict-based record and the functions around it into a class, keep callers working when the internal representation changes, and convert an object to a dict for saving.

knowledge_points.title: The same record as a dict and as a class
knowledge_points.practice: Translate dict lookups into attribute reads and back; choose which suits a described record.

knowledge_points.title: Moving a function into the class as a method
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def is_long(book):              # before: a function taking a dict
    return book["pages"] > 300

class Book:
    def __init__(self, title, pages):
        self.title = title
        self.pages = pages

    def is_long(self):          # after: a method using self
        return self.pages > 300

print(Book("Dune", 412).is_long())   # True
The dict parameter becomes self, and book["pages"] becomes self.pages.
knowledge_points.practice: Refactor two dict-taking functions into methods.

knowledge_points.title: Changing the inside without changing the callers

topics.title: Attributes by name: getattr, setattr, hasattr and vars
topics.summary: Read, set and test attributes whose names are strings, and list an object's attributes with vars().

knowledge_points.title: getattr with a name in a string
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

rex = Dog("Rex")
field = "name"
print(getattr(rex, field))          # Rex
print(getattr(rex, "age", "unknown"))  # unknown
getattr(obj, 'x') is obj.x when the name is only known at run time; the third argument is a default.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict getattr results with and without a default.

knowledge_points.title: hasattr before reading
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in hasattr checks that guard optional attributes.

knowledge_points.title: setattr from a dictionary
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Dog:
    pass

rex = Dog()
for key, value in {"name": "Rex", "age": 3}.items():
    setattr(rex, key, value)
print(rex.age)   # 3
setattr(obj, 'x', v) is obj.x = v with the name in a string.
knowledge_points.practice: Write a loop that copies a dict onto an object's attributes.

knowledge_points.title: vars() shows the attributes as a dict

topics.title: Class attributes: values shared by every instance
topics.summary: Define attributes in the class body, read them through the class or an instance, count instances, and avoid the shadowing and shared-list bugs.

knowledge_points.title: A variable in the class body is shared
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Dog:
    species = "Canis familiaris"

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

rex = Dog("Rex")
print(Dog.species, rex.species == Dog.species)   # Canis familiaris True
Instances see class attributes when they have no attribute of their own with that name.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict reads through the class and through instances; choose class vs instance attribute for described data.

knowledge_points.title: Counting instances with a class attribute
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Dog:
    count = 0

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        Dog.count += 1

Dog("Rex"); Dog("Mia")
print(Dog.count)   # 2
Update shared data through the class name, so every instance sees the change.
knowledge_points.practice: Write a counter or next-id class attribute; trace its value as objects are created.

knowledge_points.title: Assigning through self creates a shadowing instance attribute
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Dog:
    count = 0

    def __init__(self):
        self.count += 1

a = Dog(); b = Dog()
print(Dog.count, a.count, b.count)   # 0 1 1
self.count += 1 reads the class value but writes a new attribute on the instance; the class attribute never changes.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict class and instance values after shadowing; fix a counter that never counts.

knowledge_points.title: A shared list is shared by everyone
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Dog:
    tricks = []

    def add_trick(self, trick):
        self.tricks.append(trick)

a = Dog(); b = Dog()
a.add_trick("sit")
print(b.tricks)   # ['sit']
append changes the one class-level list; per-object lists belong in __init__.
knowledge_points.practice: Spot data that leaks between instances and move it into __init__.

knowledge_points.title: Double underscore: name mangling

class Account:

a = Account()
print(a._Account__pin)   # 1234

topics.title: Less boilerplate with @dataclass
topics.summary: Write a @dataclass with typed fields, use its generated __init__, __repr__ and __eq__, give fields safe defaults, and freeze it.

knowledge_points.title: Fields in, __init__ and __repr__ out
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int

print(Point(1, 2))   # Point(x=1, y=2)
Each annotated line becomes a constructor parameter and an attribute; repr is written for you.
knowledge_points.practice: Convert a hand-written class with __init__ and __repr__ into a dataclass; predict the repr.

knowledge_points.title: == compares the fields
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int

print(Point(1, 2) == Point(1, 2))   # True
The generated __eq__ compares fields in order, so you do not write it yourself.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict == between dataclass instances and between plain-class instances.

knowledge_points.title: Defaults, and default_factory for lists
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Team:
    name: str
    size: int = 0
    members: list = field(default_factory=list)

print(Team("A"))   # Team(name='A', size=0, members=[])
Writing members: list = [] raises ValueError: mutable default <class 'list'> for field members is not allowed: use default_factory.
knowledge_points.practice: Add defaults to fields; fix a dataclass that uses a list default.

knowledge_points.title: frozen=True: read-only objects
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int

p = Point(1, 2)
p.x = 5
dataclasses.FrozenInstanceError: cannot assign to field 'x'. Frozen objects can also be set members and dict keys.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which operations fail on a frozen dataclass; choose frozen or not for described data.

topics.title: Enums: a fixed set of named values
topics.summary: Define an Enum, read a member's name and value, compare members, look members up by value or name, and loop over all of them.

knowledge_points.title: Defining an Enum and reading name and value
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from enum import Enum

class Color(Enum):
    RED = 1
    GREEN = 2

print(Color.RED)                          # Color.RED
print(Color.RED.name, Color.RED.value)    # RED 1
Each class attribute becomes a member: a named, unchangeable value of type Color.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict printed members, names and values; write an Enum for a described set.

knowledge_points.title: Comparing members
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from enum import Enum

class Color(Enum):
    RED = 1
    GREEN = 2

c = Color.RED
print(c is Color.RED, c == Color.GREEN, c == 1)   # True False False
There is exactly one of each member, so is and == both work; a member never equals its plain value.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict comparisons between members and plain values; fix a comparison against the raw value.

knowledge_points.title: Looking members up by value or name
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from enum import Enum

class Color(Enum):
    RED = 1
    GREEN = 2

print(Color(2), Color["RED"])   # Color.GREEN Color.RED
Color(5)
Color(value) and Color[name] find a member; a bad value raises ValueError: 5 is not a valid Color.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict lookups, including ones that raise ValueError or KeyError.

knowledge_points.title: Looping over every member
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from enum import Enum

class Color(Enum):
    RED = 1
    GREEN = 2

for c in Color:
    print(c.name)    # RED, then GREEN
print(len(Color))    # 2
An Enum is iterable in definition order, which is handy for menus and validation.
knowledge_points.practice: Write a loop that lists all member names; predict len().

topics.title: Using enums instead of magic strings
topics.summary: Replace string constants with enum members so typos fail loudly, branch on members with match, and use auto() and StrEnum.

knowledge_points.title: Typos fail loudly with enums
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from enum import Enum

class Status(Enum):
    TODO = 1
    DONE = 2

status = "done"
print(status == "Done")    # False: silent typo
print(Status.DOEN)
A misspelt string just compares False; a misspelt member raises AttributeError: type object 'Status' has no attribute 'DOEN'.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite string-constant comparisons with an Enum; predict which typo is caught.

knowledge_points.title: match on enum members
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from enum import Enum

class Status(Enum):
    TODO = 1
    DONE = 2

def label(s):
    match s:
        case Status.TODO:
            return "to do"
        case Status.DONE:
            return "finished"

print(label(Status.DONE))   # finished
Dotted names in a case compare by value, so Status.DONE matches that member.
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the case lines; convert an elif chain on members into match.

knowledge_points.title: auto() and StrEnum
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from enum import StrEnum, auto

class Status(StrEnum):
    TODO = auto()
    DONE = auto()

print(Status.DONE.value, Status.DONE == "done")   # done True
auto() picks the values; in a StrEnum that is the lower-case name, and members compare equal to those strings (useful for JSON and input).
knowledge_points.practice: Predict auto() values for Enum and StrEnum; choose which suits reading user input.
